I've been farming this same land in Quzhou my whole life, just like my father did. I know what works here on the North China Plain. The soil is good loam, and we get enough groundwater for irrigation. There's no question what I'll grow — winter wheat and summer corn, one after the other. That's what everyone around here does. That's what the land is set up for. I'm not about to try something new at 60.

I have about 8 mu of land I work myself. My son helps during harvest but lives in Handan now. So I keep things manageable.

For wheat, I'll buy improved seed from the county agricultural supply shop — something like Jimai 22 or whatever the agronomist there recommends from the local trial plots. I'm not chasing new hybrids or spending extra money on something unproven. I'll rotary till after the corn comes off in October, then broadcast some diammonium phosphate before seeding. Come spring, I'll top-dress with urea. I need to irrigate — the rainfall here isn't reliable enough. I'll water before winter sets in, again at jointing, and once more at heading. That's three times, like I always do. I'll spray twice: once for aphids in spring, once for powdery mildew if it shows up.

For corn, I plant right after wheat harvest in June, no-till straight into the stubble — saves me time and the moisture stays in. I use hybrid seed, always have for the past twenty years. Zhengdan 958 has been good to me. I put down less fertilizer on corn than wheat, mostly urea in two splits. Two irrigations if the summer is dry, sometimes just one if we get decent rain in July. Spray once for corn borer. That's enough.

I'm not trying to maximize every kilogram. I'm trying to get a decent crop without wearing out my body or spending more than I earn.
